name: Understanding loop performance
description: A guided example: why the loop Base takes 4 cycles per iteration on processor B4. Latency and throughput bounds, simulation, critical path and timeline, with optional in-depth cards.

steps.title: Why does a loop take the time it takes?
steps.description:
This tutorial follows one real example.
It has selected the program {{program}}, the processor {{processor}} and N = {{N}}.
Cards with ▶ Show me can act on the simulator for you, or you can do it yourself.
At some topics you can open an In depth card first.
When the tutorial ends, your previous program, processor and N are restored.

steps.title: The loop: {{program}}
steps.description:
Hover the header of the table to see the C code: the loop adds
the elements of two vectors, V and W, into sum.
One iteration is written as 7 simple machine instructions:
• two loads: {{instr.0}} and {{instr.2}}
• two floating-point additions: {{instr.1}} (twice)
• the loop control: {{instr.4}}, {{instr.5}}, {{instr.6}}.

steps.title: In depth: the program
steps.description:
• The type button switches the columns: type, operation and size,
   or latency and eligible ports.
• Hover an instruction to see what it does (memory access, operands).
• Hover the header to see the C code of the loop.
• Not modeled: registers and memory ordering. Conditional branches
   (if c skip k) are taken and mispredicted with given probabilities.
• After a simulation, the first column shows how much each
   instruction contributes to the critical path.

steps.title: A chain that crosses iterations
steps.description:
Instructions 1 and 3 read and write the same variable, sum.
Addition 3 needs the result of addition 1, and addition 1 of the next
iteration needs the result of addition 3: 1 → 3 → 1 → 3 → …
This cyclic chain of dependences cannot be overlapped across iterations,
however many resources the processor has.

steps.title: Check: cyclic chains
steps.questionText: Which instructions of {{program}} belong to a cyclic chain (a variable computed from its own previous value)?

answers.explanation: Yes: each addition uses the sum of the previous one.
Yes: i is computed from its previous value (a 1-cycle chain).
They read i, but no load uses a value produced by itself.
c is computed from i, but c is not used to compute c again.

steps.title: The processor: {{processor}}
steps.description:
{{processor}} is described by a few numbers (operation types now shown):
• Dispatch {{dispatch}} and Retire {{retire}} instructions per cycle; ROB: {{rob}} instructions in flight.
• Each port starts one instruction per cycle: P0 executes the loads and stores,
   FLOAT.ADD runs on P1 or P3.
• Latencies: a load takes {{latency.MEM.LOAD}} cycles, an addition FLOAT.ADD {{latency.FLOAT.ADD}}.

steps.title: In depth: the processor
steps.description:
• Click a cell of the diagram to change it: dispatch, retire, ROB, cache,
   branch penalty, ports, and the latency of an operation type.
• A second click on a cell pins its explanation.
• 💾 saves the modified processor with a name; ✱ ↶ discards the changes.
• The Scheduler is an option of the simulation: greedy issues the oldest
   ready instructions; optimal chooses the best combination of ports.

steps.title: Latency bound
steps.description:
Each row is a cyclic chain of dependences.
The chain of sum has two additions of {{latency.FLOAT.ADD}} cycles per iteration: {{chain.sum}} cycles/iter.
The chain of i needs {{chain.i}} cycle/iter.
The longest chain gives the latency bound: {{latencyBound}} cycles/iter.
▶ Show me selects the chain of sum and draws it in the dependence graph (in red).

steps.title: In depth: the dependence graph
steps.description:
• 📈 Dependence graph opens a movable, resizable window.
• One box per loop iteration; cyclic dependences are drawn in red.
• Clicking a row of Latency bounds highlights its chain.
• Hovering an instruction number highlights it in the graph and program.
• Mouse wheel: zoom · drag: move · double click: whole graph.

steps.title: Throughput bound
steps.description:
Each row is a resource and the work it must do in one iteration.
The two loads can only use P0: 2 instructions / 1 port = {{resource.P0}} cycles/iter.
Dispatch: 7 instructions / {{dispatch}} per cycle = {{resource.Dispatch}}; retire: {{resource.Retire}}.
The busiest resource gives the throughput bound: {{throughputBound}} cycles/iter.

steps.title: In depth: sets of ports
steps.description:
• An instruction that can run on P0 or P2 does not load P0 alone:
   it only counts for sets that contain both ports.
• Numbers in grey are instructions that can escape to
   another port (hover to see which ones).
• Sets of ports are listed when they share instructions:
   P0+P2 and P2+P3 give P0+P2+P3.

steps.title: Check: minimum time
steps.questionText:
For {{program}} on {{processor}}, the latency bound is {{latencyBound}} and the throughput bound {{throughputBound}} cycles/iter.
What is the minimum time per iteration?
steps.numericCorrect: Right: max({{latencyBound}}, {{throughputBound}}) = {{minTime}}. The loop is {{boundType}}-bound: the chain of sum limits it, not the resources.
steps.numericWrong: The bounds do not add up and are not averaged: the slowest constraint wins (the maximum).

steps.title: Run the simulation
steps.description:
Now measure it. Click Run Simulation (or ▶ Show me):
the simulator executes N = {{N}} iterations of {{program}} on {{processor}}, cycle by cycle.

validation.message: Run the simulation (or click ▶ Show me) to continue

steps.title: Simulation results
steps.description:
{{simIterations}} iterations took {{cycles}} cycles: {{cyclesPerIter}} cycles/iter,
practically the minimum time predicted by the latency bound ({{minTime}}).
IPC = {{ipc}}: the 7 instructions of each iteration every ~{{cyclesPerIter|0}} cycles.
The bounds explain the performance of this loop.

steps.title: In depth: simulation results
steps.description:
• IPC: instructions per cycle.
• Primary misses start a block fill; secondary ones join a fill in progress.
• MM transfers: main-memory reads + writes (hover for the detail).
• The diagram shows how busy dispatch, each port, the cache and retire are.
• Store Results keeps a run; hover its name to see program, N and processor.

steps.title: Usage of the resources
steps.description:
The diagram shows how busy each resource was.
Dispatch used {{dispatchUsage}}% of its capacity, and retire {{retireUsage}}%.
Ports: P0 {{port.P0}}%, P1 {{port.P1}}%, P2 {{port.P2}}%, P3 {{port.P3}}%, P4 {{port.P4}}%.
No resource is saturated: the processor is mostly waiting for the additions.

steps.title: Check: usage of P1
steps.questionText: Port P1 was busy {{port.P1}}% of the cycles. Why?

answers.text: It starts the 2 additions of each iteration, and an iteration takes ~{{cyclesPerIter|0}} cycles
answers.explanation: Yes: 2 additions every {{cyclesPerIter}} cycles keep P1 busy about half of the cycles (a port starts one instruction per cycle).

answers.text: An addition occupies P1 during its {{latency.FLOAT.ADD}} cycles of latency
answers.explanation: No: ports are pipelined. P1 can start a new instruction every cycle, even if the previous one has not finished.

answers.text: Half of the additions run on P3
answers.explanation: No: P3 was busy only {{port.P3}}% of the cycles.

answers.text: P1 waits for the loads of P0
answers.explanation: Waiting does not count as usage: usage counts the cycles in which the port starts an instruction.

steps.title: The critical path
steps.description:
After the simulation, the first column shows each instruction's share of the critical path.
The two additions take {{critical.1}}% and {{critical.3}}% of it.
From iteration {{patternFrom}} to {{patternTo}} the critical path repeats the same pattern:
{{patternCycles}} critical cycles per iteration, the two additions of {{latency.FLOAT.ADD}} cycles.

steps.title: The timeline
steps.description:
Cycle by cycle: what each instruction is doing (rows: instructions, columns: cycles).
D dispatch · L load · E execute · W write result · R retire.
The critical path is in red: the first load (L L L L), then the E E of each addition.
Addition 3 waits (.) for addition 1, and addition 1 of the next iteration waits for addition 3.

steps.title: In depth: waiting symbols
steps.description:
• . waits for a source operand (data dependence)
• * waits for a free port (port conflict)
• - already executed, waits for older instructions to retire
• With a cache: ! cache/MM slot · : block fill · 2 fill in progress
   · @ cache return queue
• x: wrong path of a mispredicted branch (squashed)
• Ports and Cache add rows with resource usage; Fit fills the width.

steps.title: Dispatch runs ahead
steps.description:
Instructions are dispatched faster than the additions can execute.
Their rows of - (executed, waiting to retire in program order) grow longer and longer,
until the ROB is full ({{rob}} instructions, about 9 iterations).
From then on, an iteration can only enter when another one retires: one every {{cyclesPerIter|0}} cycles.

steps.title: Check: reading the timeline
steps.questionText: An instruction shows D . . . E W R in the timeline. Why does it wait after being dispatched?

answers.text: It waits for a source operand produced by an older instruction
answers.explanation: Yes: "." means a data dependence; it executes (E) when the operand is ready.

answers.text: It waits for a free execution port
answers.explanation: A port conflict is shown with "*".

answers.text: It waits for older instructions to retire
answers.explanation: That is "-", and it appears after the result is written (W).

answers.text: It waits for a cache miss
answers.explanation: Cache waits are shown with "!", ":", "2" or "@".

steps.title: Predict: a faster addition
steps.questionText: If FLOAT.ADD took 1 cycle instead of {{latency.FLOAT.ADD}}, what would be the minimum time per iteration of {{program}} on {{processor}}?
nextLabels: In depth: check it in the simulator
steps.numericCorrect: Right: the chain of sum would take 1 + 1 = 2 cycles/iter, the same as the throughput bound of P0 (2 loads / 1 port): the loop would be limited by both.
steps.numericWrong: Compute both bounds again: the chain of sum has two additions, and P0 still executes two loads per iteration.

steps.title: In depth: check the prediction
steps.description:
▶ Show me changes the latency of FLOAT.ADD to 1 cycle in {{processor}}
(only in the Processor panel: ✱ ↶ discards it, and the tutorial restores it at the end)
and runs the simulation again.
Last simulation: {{cyclesPerIter}} cycles/iter with FLOAT.ADD = {{latency.FLOAT.ADD}} cycle(s)
(before ▶ Show me, the result with the original latency).
